stage_description: Guinea pigs are born remarkably mature: pups arrive fully furred, with open eyes and teeth already in place, and can walk and sample solid food within their first days of life. The early stage covers roughly the first three weeks, while the youngster still relies mainly on its mother's milk but begins nibbling hay and pellets alongside her almost immediately. Weaning happens by around the third week. It is a period of rapid growth in which warmth, calm, and constant access to food and clean water matter most.
nutrition: The foundation is the mother's milk, but from the first days a pup should have constant access to hay and a specialised young-animal pellet. Growing guinea pigs do well on alfalfa hay and alfalfa-based pellets, which are richer in calcium and protein. Guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so the diet must supply stabilised vitamin C from the very start or scurvy can develop. Always provide fresh, clean water.
activity: Pups are active from birth and begin exploring within their first days. Keep the youngster with its mother and littermates in a warm, secure enclosure with no ledges to fall from or gaps to become trapped in. Soft bedding, hide houses, and a quiet setting reduce stress. Guinea pigs are intensely social, and early company from their own kind is important for normal behaviour.
veterinary_check_frequency: An early visit to a vet experienced with exotics and rodents is advisable soon after weaning or purchase. The vet will assess overall development, the bite, and skin and coat, and confirm there are no congenital problems. Weigh the pup daily on a kitchen scale: steady weight gain is the single best sign of wellbeing at this age.
dental_care: A pup's incisors erupt before birth, and all of its teeth grow continuously throughout life. Introducing unlimited hay early drives the natural tooth wear that keeps the bite forming correctly.
warning_signs: Seek a vet immediately if a pup fails to gain weight or loses weight, refuses to eat, seems limp or cold to the touch, or has diarrhoea, eye or nose discharge, or laboured breathing. In animals this small, condition deteriorates very fast, so delay is dangerous.
